title: Will It Be Me?
subtitle: Dementia Risk, Genetic Testing, and Planning Ahead for Your Family
thesis: A relative's dementia hands you a question, not a verdict: what it means for you and your children depends on which form runs in the family, whether a gene causes it or only raises the odds, and what each number really describes. Read clearly, with a genetic counselor beside you, that risk becomes a series of decisions about testing, protection, care, work, money and your own future that a family can make now, even though no test or habit can promise who will or will not become ill.
back_cover:
When your mother, your brother or your grandfather has dementia, a question follows you home from every appointment: will it be me—and will it be my children?

Will It Be Me? is a guide for families, with their stories inside it. Following composite families who live with early-onset Alzheimer's, frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's that came late, it explains in plain words which dementias are inherited and which are not, the difference between a gene that causes the disease and a gene that only raises the odds, and what each number you hear really says. It walks you through genetic counseling and testing: why the person who is ill is usually tested first, what to put in place before a blood draw, and how people live with a positive, a negative or an uncertain answer.

It shows how to recognize a change that looks like something else and get a diagnosis taken seriously, and how to build a family plan for care, work, money and legal papers, and for your own future. Its practical guidance is for the United States. It will not tell you whether to be tested, and no test, habit or program in it can promise that dementia will pass you by. What it offers is clarity, and a way to turn waiting into decisions you can make now.

parts.title: The Genetic Test, Before and After

chapters.title: The Question You Carry Home
chapters.summary: Opens with the question most readers carry out of a neurologist's office and says plainly what this book can answer and what only a genetic counselor or a doctor can. It introduces the composite families who return in every chapter, declared as composites, and shows how the five parts turn waiting into decisions.
beats: Opening scene: Dana Reyes in a hospital parking garage, four years ago, minutes after her mother Carmen was told at 52 that she has early-onset Alzheimer's; the question Dana cannot say aloud—will it be me, and my children?

The cast, declared as composites drawn from many families and resembling no real one: the Reyes family, where a gene causes the disease (Carmen, widowed; her daughter Dana, 36, married, with a daughter of 13 and a son of 9; her son Luis, 31); the Harper family, where frontotemporal dementia looked like something else for years and the genetic test gave no clear answer (Tom, whose changes began at 54; his wife Ellen; their daughter Kate, 30); the Bell family, where Alzheimer's came late and a risk gene turned up by accident (June, diagnosed at 84; her son Ray, 62, her caregiver; her grandson Marcus, 33).

What the book does and does not do: it explains and prepares decisions; it gives no individual medical or genetic advice, never says whether to be tested, recommends no drug or program, and promises no prevention; its practical information is for the United States and is dated, with where to check.

How it is built: reading your family history and its numbers, the genetic test before and after, recognizing change and getting a diagnosis, the family plan, your own years ahead; every number and medical term explained the first time it appears.
How to read it: in order, or, if the person who is ill has no diagnosis yet, starting with Part Three.

chapters.title: Runs in the Family, or Happens in It?
chapters.summary: Separates the dementias that pass down through a single gene from the far more common ones that simply happen in families as people live longer, and shows why the age at which a relative fell ill is the strongest early clue. It comes first because every later question about risk and testing depends on which kind of story your family has.
beats: Opening scene: at his mother June's diagnosis at 84, Ray Bell asks the neurologist whether it is 'in our blood'; the answer he gets, set beside the very different conversation the Reyes family had when Carmen was diagnosed at 52.

Dementia as an umbrella word, defined once: Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, vascular and Lewy body dementia, mixed forms; which of them more often run in families and which mostly happen in them.
Early onset versus late onset: what doctors usually mean by each, and why a grandparent diagnosed at 85 is a different story from a parent diagnosed at 50.
The signals that point toward an inherited form (several relatives across generations, illness at younger ages, the same form repeating) and why a single late case, or even two, usually does not.
If the relative's diagnosis is uncertain or was never made, Part Three shows how to get one; the reading of the family story depends on it.
Ends with the first thing the reader can do: note, for each affected relative, the form named and the age when changes began.

chapters.title: When a Single Gene Causes the Disease
chapters.summary: Explains in plain words what a gene and a variant are, how a disease-causing variant passes from parent to child, and why each child has the same even chance of inheriting it whatever happened to brothers and sisters. It follows the first chapter because families with an inherited form need the mechanism before any number or test can make sense.
beats: Opening scene: after her genetic result comes back, Carmen Reyes asks her daughter Dana, 'What did I give you?', and neither of them knows what the words on the report mean.
Genes, copies and variants defined: we carry two copies of most genes, pass one of them to each child by chance, and in dominant inheritance a single altered copy can be enough to cause the disease.
The genes named once, without jargon: APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 in inherited Alzheimer's; MAPT, GRN and C9orf72 in inherited frontotemporal dementia; what they have in common and how rare they are.

Why the draw is made again, separately, for every child; why such a gene rarely skips a generation, and why it can seem to when a parent died young of something else or when a variant does not always lead to illness (reduced penetrance).
What a causative gene does not tell anyone: the exact age, the course, or whether a relative who never showed signs was a carrier.
Ends with the question to take to a genetic counselor: has a variant been found in the family, and in whom?

chapters.title: The Gene That Only Raises the Odds
chapters.summary: Explains APOE, the gene most often mentioned alongside Alzheimer's, and the difference between a version that raises the likelihood of late-onset disease and a variant that causes it. It sits right after the causative genes because readers confuse the two more than anything else in this field, and the confusion feeds much of the fear.
beats: Opening scene: Marcus Bell, 33, finally opens the health section of an ancestry app he bought for fun and reads that he carries one copy of APOE e4.
APOE in plain words: everyone carries two copies, in versions called e2, e3 and e4; what carrying one or two copies of e4 does to the odds, and what it does not.
Why many people with e4 never develop Alzheimer's and many without it do, and why doctors do not use APOE alone to predict illness in an individual.
Why an APOE result adds little in a family with a causative variant, and why late onset with an e4 is a different question from early onset with PSEN1.
Ends with what Marcus can sensibly do with the result, and what it does not ask of him.

chapters.title: The Relatives Nobody Counted
chapters.summary: Shows how to gather and read your own family history, including the relatives whose illness was misnamed, hidden or cut short by something else. It comes after the genetics because the reader now knows which details matter, and before the numbers because no risk estimate is better than the history behind it.
beats: Opening scene: in a box of papers, Ellen Harper finds the state hospital record of Tom's father, admitted in his fifties for a 'nervous breakdown' and never seen by a neurologist.

The relatives who hide in a family tree: those labeled senile, depressed, alcoholic or difficult; those who died young of heart disease or an accident before any change could show; adoption, donor conception and estrangement.

Where to look and whom to ask: older relatives, death certificates, old medical records, obituaries, an autopsy report; questions that bring out useful details without turning a visit into an interrogation.
What makes a pattern and what does not, and why a counselor wants three generations, ages at onset and causes of death.
When the history is missing or cannot be recovered, and what that does to the picture.
Ends with the family history the reader can put together before any appointment, as notes in their own words rather than a form.

chapters.title: Numbers That Frighten, Numbers That Inform
chapters.summary: Translates the numbers families hear ('fifty-fifty', 'twice the risk', 'increased risk') into plain statements about how many people out of a hundred like you, and explains absolute versus relative risk and age as the largest factor of all. It closes Part One because the reader now has the history and the genetics to put a number in its place, a skill needed before deciding anything about a test.
beats: Opening scene: Luis Reyes tells his sister their odds are 'a coin toss, so whatever'; Dana answers that a coin toss at 31 is not the same as a coin toss at 55.
Absolute versus relative risk: why 'twice the risk' can mean a small change or a large one, and the question that always reveals which: twice of what?
Age as the largest factor for everyone; lifetime risk explained; why figures from studies describe groups, not you.

For families with a causative variant: how the chance falls with each year a person passes the family's usual age of onset without signs, and why that calculation belongs with a counselor, not an online calculator.
Turning a percentage into something you can decide with: picturing a hundred people like you, and asking what the number would change about what you do.
Ends with what to ask whenever a doctor, a website or an app hands you a number.

chapters.title: Why Testing Starts With the Person Who Is Ill
chapters.summary: Explains the order in which genetic testing usually happens in a family: first a diagnostic test of the person who has the disease, then, if a cause is found, predictive testing for relatives at risk. It opens Part Two because the first step most families want, testing the children, usually cannot tell them anything until this one is done.
beats: Opening scene: Ellen Harper calls a genetics clinic to have her daughter Kate tested, 'and the grandchildren, when they come'; the counselor gently asks first about Tom.

Diagnostic testing in the person who is ill: what is looked for, who orders it, and how consent works when understanding is changing; Carmen Reyes, years earlier, agreeing to give blood 'for my kids'.
Predictive testing for relatives at risk, defined: possible once the family's variant is known, and offered to adults who choose it.
When the person who is ill has died or cannot be tested: stored samples, other affected relatives, brain donation and autopsy, and what remains possible without them.
What the first test may cost and whether insurance tends to pay, with the warning that coverage varies by plan and must be checked.
Ends with the conversation to have with the ill relative's doctor, or within the family, about whether that first test has been done.

chapters.title: Positive, Negative, Uncertain: Reading a Result
chapters.summary: Walks through what a genetic report actually says: a disease-causing variant, a negative that may or may not be informative, and a 'variant of uncertain significance'. It follows the testing order because the category of the first result decides what every relative can and cannot learn next.
beats: Opening scene: at the results visit, Tom and Ellen Harper hear the phrase 'variant of uncertain significance', and Ellen asks the only question she has: so is it genetic or not?
The categories labs use (pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain, likely benign, benign), each explained with what it means for the person tested and for relatives.
Why a negative in an ill person is often uninformative, while a negative in a relative tested for a known family variant is a real answer; the contrast with Carmen Reyes's clear finding in PSEN1.
Why labs reclassify variants as knowledge grows, why a VUS is not 'half positive', and why it should not be used to test relatives.
What no report can tell anyone: when, how fast, or how severe.
Ends with how to read the sections of a lab report, and what to ask the counselor about each.

chapters.title: The DNA Kit Result You Never Asked For
chapters.summary: Explains what direct-to-consumer DNA tests look at, what they miss, and what to do when one reports an APOE result you never meant to receive. It follows the chapter on reading results because a consumer report looks like a medical one and is not.
beats: Opening scene: Marcus Bell takes the printout from his ancestry app to a genetic counselor and realizes halfway through that his e4 came from his father or his mother.

What consumer tests typically report about dementia (usually APOE), what they do not look at (most causative variants), and why a reassuring consumer result says nothing to a family with a known variant.
Raw data uploaded to third-party websites: why alarming findings are often false alarms, and why any result that matters needs a clinical-grade test.
Privacy settings and choices: what consumer companies may keep and share, research consent, deleting data and samples.
What one person's result reveals about relatives who never chose to know.
Ends with what to do when such a result arrives: whether and how to have it checked, and whom to tell.

chapters.title: Inside the Genetic Counselor's Office
chapters.summary: Describes how genetic counseling works before and after a predictive test, from the first call to the follow-up visits, and how to find a counselor. It comes before the decision chapters because the decision is meant to be made inside this process, not alone at night.
beats: Opening scene: Dana Reyes's first session, where she expects a blood draw and instead spends an hour talking about her mother, her children and what she would do with each answer.
What a genetic counselor is and does, and what a counselor will not do: tell you whether to test.

The usual steps of predictive testing for an adult-onset disease: sessions before the test, sometimes a neurological or psychological check, a support person, results given in person, follow-up afterward.
How to find a counselor (professional directories, specialist centers, telehealth), what it tends to cost, and the family history and relative's report to take along.
Why the protocol is slow on purpose, and what to do if it feels like an obstacle.
Ends with the questions worth raising at a first session.

chapters.title: Reasons to Know, and Reasons Not To
chapters.summary: Lays out, without taking a side, the reasons people give for having a predictive test and the reasons they give for not having one, including the recognized right not to know. It follows counseling because the reader now knows what the process asks, and can weigh what it would give back.
beats: Opening scene: Ray Bell tells his son Marcus not to tell him what the APOE result says about him: 'I've watched my mother. Knowing won't change a thing I do.'
Reasons people choose to know: planning work, money and family; decisions about children; ending a doubt that already shapes life; eligibility for some research; relief if the answer is negative.
Reasons people choose not to: the lack of a treatment that stops the disease, insurance not yet in place, the weight of a future without a date, wanting the present to stay the present.
The right not to know, and how families can respect it; Luis Reyes's reasons, set beside his sister's.
Why the decision can be revisited, and why 'not now' is a decision too.
Ends with a way to talk the decision through: what would I do differently with each answer?

chapters.title: Timing, and the Sibling Who Chooses Differently
chapters.summary: Deals with when to test, if at all, and with what happens when brothers and sisters decide differently. It follows the reasons because the same person may answer differently at thirty and at forty-five, and because a result never belongs to one person alone.
beats: Opening scene: Dana Reyes sets a test date around her children's school year and asks Luis whether he wants to hear her result; he says no.
Timing: the life stages people weigh, such as before starting a family, after insurance is in place, before a career move, or as they approach the age their parent fell ill.
Why minors are generally not tested for adult-onset conditions, and what that means for parents who want an answer for their children.
Siblings: your result does not change a brother's or sister's odds, except between identical twins; agreeing on what will be shared, and with whom.
The parent in the middle: when a young adult's test would reveal a parent's status, and how families handle it.
Ends with how to tell siblings what you have decided without asking them to decide the same.

chapters.title: The Law That Protects You, and Where It Stops
chapters.summary: Explains the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, what it protects in health insurance and most employment, and the life, disability and long-term-care insurance it leaves out. It comes before any blood draw because the order in which a person tests and applies for coverage cannot be reversed.
beats: Opening scene: Marcus Bell, filling in a long-term-care insurance application, reaches the question about genetic tests and stops.

What the federal law covers: health insurers may not use genetic information, family history included, to decide eligibility or premiums; most employers may not use it to hire, fire or promote, or ask for it.
Where it stops: life, disability and long-term-care insurance; small employers; some government and military coverage; and, once symptoms appear, the other laws that take over.
State laws that add protections, why they vary, and where to check the current rules.
Why honest answers on applications matter, and why the details are a question for an insurance professional or an attorney, not a guess.
Ends with the step many counselors ask people to consider: reviewing coverage before the test.

chapters.title: Who Will See the Result, and What to Do First
chapters.summary: Covers where a genetic result goes once it exists, from medical records and patient portals to billing and research files, and the practical arrangements to make before the result arrives. It closes the preparation chapters by turning the protections and their limits into a concrete order of things.
beats: Opening scene: three weeks before her blood draw, Dana Reyes and her husband sit at the kitchen table with their policies spread out and a list of who will be told what.
Who can see a result: the medical record, the patient portal (where results may appear before anyone calls), billing and claims, research files; what paying out of pocket does and does not change.
Options some centers offer to limit where a result is recorded, and how to ask about them.
What to arrange first: coverage reviewed, a support person chosen, the result visit planned in person, the following days kept clear.
A plan for each possible answer, thought through in your own words beforehand.
Ends with an order of steps the reader can go over with the counselor.

chapters.title: A Positive Result, and Who to Tell
chapters.summary: Follows the first weeks after a positive predictive result: what it says, what it leaves open, and how and when to tell a partner and children. It comes first among the results because it is the answer readers fear most, and the one where the order of conversations matters most.
beats: Opening scene: Dana Reyes hears the word 'positive' in her counselor's office, her husband beside her, and drives home in silence.
What a positive result for a causative variant means and does not mean: illness very likely at some point, no date, no stage, and a person who is the same today as yesterday.
The first weeks: shock, grief, sometimes relief; follow-up counseling; mental health support and when to ask for it.
Telling a partner: timing, what to say, and what the partner needs in turn.
Telling children in words that fit their age, what they need to know now and what can wait, and their own right to decide about testing as adults.
Ends with who else needs to know, who does not, and the reader's right to decide.

chapters.title: When the Result Is Negative, or Uncertain
chapters.summary: Covers the two results that are supposed to bring relief and often do not: a negative that frees a person from the family variant, and an uncertain answer that frees no one. It follows the positive result because both are lived in its shadow, often inside the same family.
beats: Opening scene: months after his sister's result, Luis Reyes is tested too, hears 'negative', and cannot bring himself to call Dana.
What a true negative means: the family variant was not passed on, his future children are not at risk from it, and the ordinary risk that comes with age remains.
Survivor's guilt among siblings: why it comes, how it shows (overwork, distance, silence), and how brothers and sisters have found their way back to each other.
Living with an uncertain answer: Kate Harper, a year after her father's VUS, still not knowing whether there is anything to know; why family history still counts when no gene is found.
Keeping a door open: asking the lab and the counselor to get back in touch if a variant is reclassified, and research that may bring answers.
Ends with the next step for each person, depending on the answer they live with.

chapters.title: When the Change Looks Like Something Else
chapters.summary: Describes the early signs of frontotemporal dementia and of Alzheimer's, why the first changes are so often taken for depression, another psychiatric illness or a midlife crisis, and when and how to insist on a neurological evaluation. It opens Part Three because many families lose years here, and because readers at risk may one day watch for these signs in someone else, or in themselves.
beats: Opening scene: Ellen Harper remembers the year Tom, then 54, bought a boat they could not afford, made remarks that shamed their daughter, and was treated for depression by a doctor who never saw him with her.
Frontotemporal dementia's early signs: changes in personality, behavior, judgment and language, often with memory spared at first.
Alzheimer's early signs: trouble with recent memory, repeated questions, getting lost in familiar tasks; and how early-onset forms can begin with other symptoms.
Why these changes get other names (depression, bipolar disorder, stress, menopause, a midlife crisis) and the clues that point to something neurological.
When to push and how: describing changes with concrete, dated examples, asking for a referral to a neurologist or memory clinic, bringing a witness, and the words that get attention.
Ends with a short account of the changes the reader can prepare for a doctor, in their own words.

chapters.title: Decoding the Scan Report Before the Doctor Calls
chapters.summary: Explains how to read the scan reports and test results that often reach families through a patient portal before anyone explains them, and describes the main types of dementia in plain words. It follows the signs because this is usually what happens next: a report arrives, full of terms nobody has defined.
beats: Opening scene: at eleven at night, Ray Bell reads his mother June's MRI report on the portal ('generalized atrophy', 'small vessel ischemic changes') and looks up every word.
Common terms on MRI, CT and PET reports explained, and why many describe changes that are ordinary for age; what amyloid and tau mean when blood or spinal fluid tests mention them.
The main types of dementia in plain words (Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, mixed dementia) and what each tends to look like in daily life.
Mild cognitive impairment and other labels that come before, or instead of, the word dementia, and what they do and do not mean.
Why a report is not a diagnosis, and what to do in the hours before the doctor's call.
Ends with how to turn the words you looked up into questions for the appointment.

chapters.title: Questions, Specialists and Second Opinions
chapters.summary: Prepares the reader for the diagnostic appointment, with the questions to bring and what a full evaluation includes, and explains when to seek a specialist center or a second opinion. It follows the report chapter because the reader now has words for what they want to ask.
beats: Opening scene: unsatisfied with a general neurologist who called Tom's diagnosis 'probably FTD', Ellen Harper books a second opinion at a specialist center several hours' drive away.
What a thorough evaluation usually involves: history from someone who knows the person well, cognitive testing, imaging, blood tests, sometimes spinal fluid or PET; what to ask if a piece is missing.
The questions to bring: which type, how certain, what else was ruled out, what to expect, whether genetic testing is advised, whom to call between visits.
Specialist centers (academic memory clinics, frontotemporal and young-onset programs, research centers) and how to find and reach one.
Second opinions: when they make sense, how to ask without burning bridges, how to have records sent.
Ends with how to leave the appointment with a written summary and a next step.

chapters.title: Who Does What: Sharing Care Without Breaking Apart
chapters.summary: Shows how families divide the work of caring for someone with dementia among siblings and a spouse, without leaving it all to whoever lives closest. It opens the family plan because every later decision about work, money and papers depends on who is doing what.
beats: Opening scene: with both their results in, Dana and Luis Reyes sit down to divide the care of their widowed mother, and Luis, the one who tested negative, offers to take on everything.
The jobs that make up care beyond the daily tasks: money, medical decisions and appointments, paperwork, presence, relief for whoever is closest; naming them so they can be shared.
A spouse's place and limits, seen through Ellen Harper; siblings at a distance and what they can carry from afar.
When the caregiver is at risk too: caring for a parent with the disease you may have inherited.
Family meetings that work, sometimes with a social worker or care manager in the room, and revisiting the plan when things change.
Ends with the first conversation to have with siblings or a partner about who takes which job.

chapters.title: Work, Leave and Money: What the Rules Allow
chapters.summary: Explains the job protections and the money that can help: federal family leave and who it covers and who it doesn't, disability benefits and the fast-track programs for early-onset conditions, and Medicaid. It comes after the division of care because once roles are clear, each person needs to know what their job and the public programs allow.
beats: Opening scene: Ray Bell learns he can take protected leave from the large company where he works to care for his mother June; his son Marcus, who helps every weekend, learns that as a grandson he is not covered.
Federal family leave: who qualifies, for which relatives, for how long, unpaid but job-protected; state paid-leave programs where they exist; Ellen Harper, at a small firm, outside the federal rule.

Disability benefits for the person who is ill, the fast-track list that includes early-onset Alzheimer's and some frontotemporal forms, and the work history they require; how Tom Harper's claim moved.
Medicaid for long-term care: what it pays for, why the rules differ by state, the look-back on transfers of money, and why an elder law attorney is worth consulting early.
Ends with the calls to make first, and where to check the figures that change every year.

chapters.title: The Papers to Sign While There Is Still Time
chapters.summary: Covers the legal documents worth signing while a person with dementia still has the capacity to do so: powers of attorney for money and health care, an advance directive, a will or trust, and releases for medical information. It follows work and money because those arrangements depend on who has the authority to act.
beats: Opening scene: in an elder law attorney's office, Tom Harper signs a durable power of attorney while Ellen watches for the moment he stops following.

The documents and what each does: financial power of attorney, health care proxy, advance directive or living will, medical information release, will or trust; later, medical orders for the end of life.
Capacity explained: why a diagnosis alone does not remove it, how a doctor's note can protect the documents, and why waiting is the most common mistake.
What happens when it is too late: guardianship or conservatorship, and what they involve.
Forms and rules that differ by state; where to get the right ones, and when a lawyer is needed.
Ends with the documents to raise at the next family meeting.

chapters.title: The Help Many Families Never Hear About
chapters.summary: Describes the help that exists and that families often find too late: support groups and specialist associations, respite care, palliative care, and hospice, including how a person with dementia qualifies. It closes the family plan because these services change what the plan can ask of each person.
beats: Opening scene: Ray Bell, exhausted, hears a nurse ask whether anyone has talked with him about hospice for his mother, and thinks she must mean someone else.
Support groups and specialist associations: national dementia organizations, frontotemporal associations, groups for young-onset families and for adult children, local agencies on aging.
Respite care: adult day programs, help at home, short stays; how families pay for it, and how to ask.
Palliative care, defined: comfort and support at any stage, alongside other care.
Hospice for dementia: how eligibility is judged, why it is hard to predict, what the Medicare benefit includes, and that it can be given at home or in a care facility.
Ends with the exact questions to ask a doctor about palliative care and hospice, and when to ask them.

chapters.title: Planning Your Own Life Under Uncertainty
chapters.summary: Turns to the reader's own future, with money, career and advance directives for yourself, whether you have tested positive, are still at risk or have chosen not to know. It opens Part Five because after planning for the person who is ill, the reader can plan for themselves with the same tools.
beats: Opening scene: Dana Reyes, a year after her result, meets a financial planner and says out loud for the first time that she may stop working before her friends do.
Career: how people weigh staying, changing course or building flexibility, and why disability coverage and retirement accounts are worth reviewing early.
Money: savings, long-term-care options, and naming someone you trust to act for you.
Advance directives for yourself, written while healthy: your agent, your values, your wishes about research and brain donation.
Living with a plan without living as if already ill; for an APOE carrier like Marcus Bell, planning in proportion to the risk.
Ends with the first conversation to have with a partner or friend about your own wishes.

chapters.title: The Question of Having Children
chapters.summary: Presents, without judgment, the decision about having children when a gene or a family history is in play, and the options people consider. It follows your own plan because for many readers this is the decision that weighs most, and it depends on what is known about the family's genetics.
beats: Opening scene: Kate Harper and her partner sit with a fertility specialist who explains what is possible when a family has no known gene.

Options people consider when a variant is known: conceiving and accepting the odds, IVF with preimplantation genetic testing, prenatal testing, donor eggs or sperm, adoption, waiting, or deciding not to have children; Dana Reyes's view, as a parent who learned her status after her children were born.
For people who do not want to learn their own status: testing approaches that protect that choice.
When no gene has been found: why the choices narrow, and what remains.
Costs, insurance and state coverage that vary widely; a genetic counselor and a fertility specialist as the people to ask.
Ends with how couples have shaped the conversation so that neither fear nor pressure makes the decision.

chapters.title: Brain Health: What the Evidence Can and Cannot Say
chapters.summary: Reports what research says about general brain health (blood pressure, physical activity, hearing, sleep and other factors studied in large populations) and what that evidence cannot promise any individual. It also helps the reader stop treating every lost word or misplaced key as a symptom, and comes late in the book because it answers the question 'is there anything I can do?' honestly.
beats: Opening scene: Marcus Bell forgets a colleague's name in a meeting, spends the evening on supplement websites, and closes the laptop angry.
What population studies of modifiable factors suggest, and why an association in a large group is not a promise to a single person; no program, diet, supplement or brain exercise is offered.
Why that evidence applies differently to a causative gene like the Reyes family's than to a risk gene like Marcus's.
Ordinary forgetting versus change: why stress, sleep loss and age explain most lapses, and the signs described in Part Three that would call for an evaluation instead.
When watching yourself becomes its own burden: asking someone you trust to tell you if they notice something, and support for anxiety.
Ends with the health care worth having for its own sake, with no promise attached.

chapters.title: Hope You Can Use: Research Open to Families
chapters.summary: Explains the family registries, observational studies and prevention trials open to people at risk, what they ask, what they give back and how to judge one, and ends with how people carry anticipatory grief and fear without letting them run their lives. It comes last because it is the honest form of hope this book can offer: decisions and participation, not a promised breakthrough.
beats: Opening scene: Kate and Ellen Harper at a research center, where Kate gives blood for a frontotemporal dementia family registry and Ellen asks about donating Tom's brain one day.
Registries, observational studies and prevention trials: what each asks of a participant, whether genetic results are shared or withheld, and what participants get back.
How to judge a study: who runs it, ethics review, costs, time, risks, what happens to your data; Dana Reyes weighing a prevention trial open to carriers.
Where to find studies, and how to ask a doctor or counselor about them.
Anticipatory grief, named: mourning someone who is still alive and fearing your own future, as people who have lived it describe it.
Ends with the ways people keep fear in its place: shared conversations, support, and lives that go on.

chapters.title: From Waiting to Deciding
chapters.summary: Returns to the three families to show where each stands and which decisions they have made, and gathers the book's central idea: a risk read clearly becomes a set of choices. It closes without promises, on the next step the reader can take.
beats: The Reyes, Harper and Bell families as the book leaves them: what each has decided, and what each still does not know.
The thread of the book: a family history read clearly, a test chosen or declined with care, change recognized, a plan in place, a life that continues.
What no one can promise, said once more, and the hope that is real.
The next step for each kind of reader, and where to find the people who can help.
